name: Bianchi Anisotropic Cosmologies
description: A family of spatially homogeneous but generally anisotropic cosmologies classified by the symmetry group of their spatial slices. They generalize FLRW models to study anisotropy in the early universe.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history:
The Bianchi universes began as a problem in pure mathematics, with no thought of cosmology. In 1898 the Italian geometer Luigi Bianchi asked how many essentially different ways a space of three dimensions can admit a continuous group of symmetries, meaning motions that carry the space rigidly into itself, and proved that there are exactly nine, classified by the structure of their symmetry algebras [bianchi1898]. This was differential geometry in the tradition of Lie and Klein, written two decades before general relativity existed and four before anyone applied it to the cosmos.¶Bianchi's classification matters to physics because of a single observation: a universe is spatially homogeneous if some symmetry group slides each spatial slice rigidly onto itself, and those groups are precisely Bianchi's nine. The Bianchi types therefore catalogue every way a universe can be the same at every point yet not the same in every direction: anisotropic generalizations of the homogeneous, isotropic Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker model. Abraham Taub wrote down the vacuum members in 1951 [taub1951], and George Ellis and Malcolm MacCallum put the subject on its modern footing in 1969, dividing the types into "class A" and "class B" according to whether a certain trace of the structure constants vanishes, the organizing scheme of the field ever since [ellismaccallum1969].¶The nine types are told apart by their structure constants, which for each symmetry group reduce to a symmetric matrix with eigenvalues $(n_1, n_2, n_3)$, each free to be positive, negative, or zero, together with a vector whose single independent component is $a$. Two rules then fix the class and the type: a type is class A when $a = 0$ and class B when $a 
eq 0$, and the type itself follows from the signs of $(n_1, n_2, n_3)$. The class and the type therefore follow from the two invariants, and the nine types, with the group and the isotropic FLRW limit each admits, are these:¶TABLE:: Type | Class | $a$ | $(n_1, n_2, n_3)$ | Group | FLRW limit ;; I | A | $0$ | $(0,0,0)$ | Abelian $\mathbb{R}^3$ | flat ($k=0$) ;; II | A | $0$ | $(+,0,0)$ | Heisenberg | none ;; III (= VI$_{-1}$) | B | $
eq 0$ | $(0,+,-)$ | unnamed | none ;; IV | B | $
eq 0$ | $(0,0,+)$ | unnamed | none ;; V | B | $
eq 0$ | $(0,0,0)$ | unnamed | open ($k<0$) ;; VI$_0$ | A | $0$ | $(0,+,-)$ | unnamed | none ;; VI$_h$ | B | $
eq 0$ | $(0,+,-)$ | unnamed | none ;; VII$_0$ | A | $0$ | $(0,+,+)$ | unnamed | flat ($k=0$) ;; VII$_h$ | B | $
eq 0$ | $(0,+,+)$ | unnamed | open ($k<0$) ;; VIII | A | $0$ | $(+,+,-)$ | $\widetilde{SL(2,\mathbb{R})}$ | none ;; IX | A | $0$ | $(+,+,+)$ | $SU(2)$ | closed ($k>0$)¶Let us define these groups precisely. The Abelian group is flat space under addition, $\mathbb{R}^3 = \{\,(x,y,z) : x,y,z \in \mathbb{R}\,\}$ with group law $(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) \mapsto \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$; every element commutes, which gives type I its flat slices. The Heisenberg group is the simplest case that does not commute, the unipotent upper triangular matrices $$H_3 = \left\{\,  egin{pmatrix} 1 & a & c \ 0 & 1 & b \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} : a, b, c \in \mathbb{R} \,ight\},$$ whose single nontrivial commutator is the canonical relation of quantum mechanics.¶The groups of types IX and VIII matter most for cosmology. The first is the special unitary group $$SU(2) = \left\{\, U \in \mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{C}) : U^\dagger U = \mathbb{1},\ \det U = 1 \,ight\},$$ the double cover of $SO(3)$ and the isometry group of the round $S^3$, which is why type IX has spherical slices and a closed FLRW limit. Its noncompact counterpart is the special linear group $$SL(2, \mathbb{R}) = \left\{\, M \in \mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R}) : \det M = 1 \,ight\},$$ whose universal cover gives the type VIII group. Because $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ is not simply connected, since it retracts onto its $SO(2)$ rotation subgroup and so has fundamental group $\pi_1 = \mathbb{Z}$, that cover, written $\widetilde{SL(2,\mathbb{R})}$, is defined as the unique simply connected Lie group sharing the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})$: an infinite cover with one sheet for each integer, one that, unlike every other group of the nine, admits no faithful matrix representation in finitely many dimensions. It plays the role for hyperbolic geometry that $SU(2)$ plays for the sphere.¶The Bianchi cosmologies turn strange in their dynamics. The class A models can be cast as a particle moving in a potential, and their behavior on the approach to the singularity ranges from the simple to the chaotic. Type I, the Kasner solution, expands along two axes while contracting along the third, a single fixed anisotropic motion. Type IX is another matter entirely: this is the Mixmaster universe, introduced by Charles Misner in 1969, whose approach to the singularity is an unending, chaotic sequence of Kasner epochs, the axes of expansion and contraction trading places in a sequence that never settles [misner1969]. The same year and shortly after, Vladimir Belinskii, Isaak Khalatnikov, and Evgenii Lifshitz advanced the conjecture that gives the Bianchi models their deepest significance: that this Mixmaster oscillation is the generic behavior of any spacetime near a singularity, type IX being one instance of it, with neighboring points decoupling so that each evolves like its own independent Bianchi IX universe [bkl1970]. If the BKL conjecture holds, the structure of the cosmic singularity is, locally and everywhere, a Bianchi cosmology.¶The diagonal type I model, $ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + a_1(t)^2dx^2 + a_2(t)^2dy^2 + a_3(t)^2dz^2$, is the member against which the rest of the family is measured. Its slices are ordinary flat space, so the three scale factors are the whole of the geometry and the whole of the anisotropy, and the shape of the curvature is easy to say: expansion along an axis is carried by $a_i''/a_i$ and the shear between two axes by the product of their expansion rates. We take the Ricci and Einstein tensors for arbitrary scale factors, because the useful case is type I with matter in it, where the time component of the Einstein tensor returns the density and the three spatial components return three separate pressures, one per axis. Without the matter, the same four equations force the scale factors to be powers of the time whose exponents sum to one along with their squares, the Kasner solution. Type I with a fluid and Kasner's vacuum belong to one family, and in type IX the family can no longer be solved in closed form and becomes the Mixmaster universe.¶A classification of symmetric spaces from the nineteenth century became the framework for anisotropic cosmology, for tests of the cosmological principle, and for the study of the singularity at the beginning of time. It is the complete list of homogeneous cosmologies, and the very nearly isotropic universe we observe sits inside it as a special, finely tuned member, which is why cosmologists need the whole family. The family supplies the alternatives against which isotropy can be measured, and with them the question "how anisotropic could the early universe have been, and how do we know it wasn't?"

related.text: The isotropic case, with one scale factor in place of three. Types I and VII$_0$ hold the flat universe, V and VII$_h$ the open one, and IX the closed one [ellismaccallum1969].
The vacuum of type I, two axes stretching and one squeezing at fixed exponents [kasner1921].
Type IX in vacuum, which Charles Misner named in 1969 after a kitchen mixer [misner1969].
Abraham Taub's vacuum of 1951 is type IX with two axes equal, and it extends through a horizon into the NUT region [taub1951, misner1963].
The homogeneous cosmologies outside Bianchi's classification, with space $\mathbb{R} \times S^2$ [kantowski1966, ellismaccallum1969].

Where the expanding Bianchi universes end up when the cosmological constant is positive. Robert Wald proved in 1983 that every type but IX approaches de Sitter space exponentially, and that type IX does too when $\Lambda$ is large enough [wald1983].
Type I filled with a stiff fluid or a massless scalar field, whose three scale factors are powers of the time [jacobs1968, belinskii1973].

A vacuum whose group of four symmetries holds groups of Bianchi's types I and VII. They act on surfaces with a time direction in them, so the spacetime is the same at every time as well [gibbons2008petrov, terzis2009].

A flat universe of spinning dust in the Einstein-Cartan theory, which turns round where a big bang would be. The Bianchi universes of types I to VIII filled with the same dust can avoid the singularity too, where the torsion outweighs the shear [tafel1973, kopczynski1973].

Friedmann universes whose space is a torus, which keeps the homogeneity of space and gives up its isotropy. Ya. B. Zel'dovich and A. A. Starobinskii put a universe that expands at three different rates on such a torus in 1984 [zeldovich1984].
Bianchi type I holding a uniform magnetic field and no matter, the universe Gerald Rosen found in 1962 [rosen1962, jacobs1969].

coordinates.name: Type I, Cartesian

parameters.description: Scale factor along $z$ ($a_3 > 0$); the three are independent, and the model is isotropic only where they agree

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ a cosmic time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ comoving Cartesian lengths, and the three scale factors $a_1(t)$, $a_2(t)$, and $a_3(t)$ are arbitrary, positive, and dimensionless. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a prime is the derivative with respect to that chart time, $a_i' = \dfrac{da_i}{d(ct)} = \dfrac{1}{c}\dfrac{da_i}{dt}$ and $a_i'' = \dfrac{1}{c^2}\dfrac{d^2a_i}{dt^2}$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
